claims.text: Rhythm control (AF): class Ia, Ic or III drugs can convert AF to sinus rhythm;
claims.quote: Medications for conversion of atrial fibrillation to sinus rhythm include class Ia (procainamide, quinidine, disopyramide), class Ic (flecainide, propafenone), and class III (amiodarone, dofetilide, dronedarone, ibutilide, sotalol, vernakalant) antiarrhythmics

claims.text: except amiodarone and sotalol, which also slow the rate, don't use them until the rate is controlled;
claims.quote: Excepting amiodarone and sotalol, which also slow ventricular response rate to atrial fibrillation, these medications should not be used until the rate has been controlled.

claims.text: oral forms also maintain sinus rhythm (amiodarone most effective, but more adverse events).
claims.quote: A Cochrane review found antiarrhythmic medication efficacy ranged from 33% to 57%, with amiodarone being most effective (4). Nevertheless, antiarrhythmic medication for this purpose was associated with more adverse events, including mortality.

claims.text: In flutter, class Ia/Ic can allow 1:1 conduction, so control the rate first with BB or non-DHP CCB.
claims.quote: If medication is used to restore sinus rhythm, rate must first be controlled with beta-blockers or nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (eg, verapamil, diltiazem). Many of the antiarrhythmic medications that can restore sinus rhythm (especially class Ia and Ic) can slow atrial flutter, shorten AV nodal refractoriness (by their vagolytic effects), or do both enough to allow 1:1 conduction with paradoxical increase in ventricular rate and hemodynamic compromise.

claims.text: AF/AFL rate control: the least effective rate-control drug, but may be preferred when HF is present;
claims.quote: Digoxin is the least effective but may be preferred if heart failure is present.

claims.text: with antiarrhythmics for flutter, it is one of the AV-nodal drugs given alongside.
claims.quote: These medications may be used for long-term maintenance as required to prevent recurrence in association with medication to prolong AV nodal refractoriness (class II, III, IV, or digoxin) (1).

claims.text: Before elective cardioversion of AF, consider reducing or holding digoxin 1–2 days;
claims.quote: It may be desirable to reduce the dose of or discontinue LANOXIN for 1 to 2 days prior to electrical cardioversion of atrial fibrillation to avoid the induction of ventricular arrhythmias
claims.locator: 5.4 Risk of Ventricular Arrhythmias During Electrical Cardioversion

claims.text: delay elective cardioversion if digoxin toxicity is suspected.
claims.quote: If digitalis toxicity is suspected, elective cardioversion should be delayed.
claims.locator: 5.4 Risk of Ventricular Arrhythmias During Electrical Cardioversion

claims.text: Dose: individualized by age, lean body weight, renal function and other drugs;
claims.quote: LANOXIN dose is based on patient-specific factors (age, lean body weight, renal function, etc.).

claims.text: if loading, give half the total load first, then ¼ every 6–8 h twice;
claims.quote: administer half the total loading dose initially, then ¼ the loading dose every 6-8 hours twice
claims.locator: 2.2 Loading Dosing Regimen in Adults and Pediatric Patients

claims.text: lower maintenance doses in renal impairment.
claims.quote: patients with impaired renal function require smaller than usual maintenance doses of digoxin

claims.text: Serum level: <0.5 ng/mL loses efficacy and >2 ng/mL adds toxicity without benefit;
claims.quote: Serum digoxin levels less than 0.5 ng/mL have been associated with diminished efficacy, while levels above 2 ng/mL have been associated with increased toxicity without increased benefit.
claims.locator: 2.5 Monitoring to Assess Safety, Efficacy, and Therapeutic Blood Levels

claims.text: draw just before the next dose or ≥6 h after the last dose,
claims.quote: Obtain serum digoxin concentrations just before the next scheduled LANOXIN dose or at least 6 hours after the last dose.
claims.locator: 2.5 Monitoring to Assess Safety, Efficacy, and Therapeutic Blood Levels

claims.text: and don't change the dose on one isolated level.
claims.quote: do not use an isolated measurement of serum digoxin concentration as the basis for increasing or decreasing the LANOXIN dose
claims.locator: 2.5 Monitoring to Assess Safety, Efficacy, and Therapeutic Blood Levels

claims.text: Toxicity: nausea, vomiting, visual changes and arrhythmias;
claims.quote: Indicated by nausea, vomiting, visual disturbances, and cardiac arrhythmias.

claims.text: bidirectional VT, nonparoxysmal junctional tachycardia in AF and hyperkalemia are serious signs;
claims.quote: Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, nonparoxysmal junctional tachycardia in the presence of atrial fibrillation, and hyperkalemia are serious signs of digitalis toxicity.

claims.text: hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia allows toxicity at lower levels.
claims.quote: If hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia (often due to diuretic use) is present, lower doses and serum levels can still cause toxicity

claims.text: Stop digoxin, monitor,
claims.quote: discontinue LANOXIN and place the patient on a cardiac monitor
Correct hypokalemia by administering potassium so that serum potassium is maintained between 4.0 and 5.5 mmol/L.

claims.text: Digoxin Immune Fab for life-threatening arrhythmias or hyperkalemia;
claims.quote: Life threatening arrhythmias (ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, high degree A-V block, bradyarrhythma, sinus arrest) or hyperkalemia requires administration of Digoxin Immune Fab.

claims.text: atropine for bradycardia/heart block;
claims.quote: Bradycardia and heart block caused by digoxin are parasympathetically mediated and respond to atropine.

claims.text: not removed by dialysis.
claims.quote: Digoxin is not effectively removed from the body by dialysis because of its large extravascular volume of distribution.

claims.text: Counsel: report nausea, vomiting, persistent diarrhea, confusion, weakness or visual changes (blurred or green-yellow vision, halos), which can mean the dose is too high.
claims.quote: Advise patients to contact their doctor or a health care professional if they experience nausea, vomiting, persistent diarrhea, confusion, weakness, or visual disturbances (including blurred vision, green-yellow color disturbances, halo effect) as these could be signs that the dose of LANOXIN may be too high.
